name: JLL on AI in Commercial Real Estate: Research, Surveys and Guidance
title: JLL on AI in Commercial Real Estate: Research, Surveys and Guidance
answer: JLL's website publishes research, surveys and guidance on AI in commercial real estate, including a 2025 technology survey of over 1,000 senior decision-makers across 16 markets. Its most striking finding is that the share of companies running CRE AI pilots rose from 5% to 92% in three years, while only 5% report achieving most programme goals, a gap between experimentation and results that frames much of the site's other material.

sections.body: JLL, the commercial real estate services firm, publishes these pages as insights, research and guidance for corporate real estate decision-makers. The material spans several documents: a 2025 Global Real Estate Technology Survey of more than 1,000 senior CRE decision-makers across 16 markets; the biennial Global Future of Work survey, produced since 2011, whose 2024 edition drew on more than 2,300 CRE decision-makers; field research by JLL's Future Vision team with over 40 senior executives, entrepreneurs and academics; and articles on AI risk, physical AI and sustainable retrofits. The pages carry no single publication date beyond the survey years they cite.
sections.heading: What this source is

sections.body: The technology survey reports that the number of companies running CRE AI pilots exploded from 5% to 92% in three years, with technologies such as environmental sensors, data modelling tools and predictive maintenance adopted by over 80% of large occupiers. Research identified around 27 AI use cases across the CRE value chain, with occupiers pursuing an average of five pilots at once, prioritising portfolio optimisation, energy management and data workflows. Yet only 5% report achieving most programme goals. The Future of Work material finds 90% of companies planning to integrate AI to support human experts over five years, 73% of CRE professionals already using AI to augment daily work, and an ecosystem of more than 700 PropTech companies. A separate article argues AI operates through role augmentation, selective displacement and job creation, with displacement moderate and concentrated, and hiring restraint largely anticipatory. JLL's risk guidance notes data security, privacy and intellectual property as the biggest technology challenge, and warns that employees may upload proprietary information into public models. JLL also describes JLL GPT, its generative AI built for CRE, and the Falcon platform.
sections.heading: What it says

sections.body: The source gives many figures: AI pilots rising from 5% to 92% in three years, with only 5% achieving most programme goals; over 80% adoption of sensors, data modelling and predictive maintenance among large occupiers; around 27 AI use cases and an average of five simultaneous pilots; 90.1% expecting a Hybrid 2.0 approach over five years, against 5.3% staying manual and 4.6% aiming to fully automate; 89% of leaders believing AI can solve major CRE challenges; 73% of professionals using AI daily; over 700 PropTech companies; 65% of sustainable asset improvement tasks potentially optimised by AI; light to medium retrofits unlocking 10% to 40% energy savings, or $0.49 to $1.94 per square foot; retrofit rates needing to triple for net zero by 2050; over 13,000 humanoids shipped in 2025; a physical AI market near $900 billion by 2035; and robotics investment growing from $670 million in 2015 to $28 billion.
sections.heading: Figures and claims worth noting

sections.body: For a reader following AI in real estate, this source supplies the adoption evidence behind the claim that the large commercial services firms run enterprise AI. It quantifies how quickly occupiers moved from planning to piloting, names the use cases they prioritise, and documents the gap between piloting and realised goals. It also covers the risk side, including data leakage through public models and the sandbox and governance responses, and looks ahead to physical AI and robotics in facilities management, where JLL argues buildings designed for robotics will command rent premiums.
sections.heading: What it means for AI in Real Estate

sections.body: The material is published by JLL, a commercial real estate services firm with its own AI products, including JLL GPT and the Falcon platform, so its framing of opportunity and its advocacy of early adoption serve its commercial position. Several pages are undated beyond the survey years they cite, and the physical AI projections to 2035 and 2040 rest on third-party forecasts from Barclays, PitchBook, Forbes and the World Economic Forum. The coverage concentrates on large corporate occupiers and investors, with little on smaller landlords or residential real estate.
